public_rationale: The data-scarcity concern has support: Epoch estimated that continued scaling would use the available stock of human-generated public text between 2026 and 2032. That is an approaching constraint, not existing exhaustion. The broad capability-plateau claim is contradicted by post-March improvements on independent abstract-reasoning tests and developer mathematics, science and coding evaluations. Gains were uneven and sometimes required more inference compute; METR's autonomy results provide an important qualification.
limitations: Support for data scarcity depends on the ordinary human-text reading and continuation of scaling trends.
Synthetic and other data sources prevent treating this as exhaustion of all training data.
Improved benchmark performance does not imply improvement on every real-world task or at fixed cost.

statement.excerpt: They're running out of training data, and the actual capabilities of these models were peaking as far back as March 2024.

from_speaker: peaking as far back as March 2024
our_interpretation: The data clause ordinarily means usable human-produced training text was becoming a constraint on continued scaling, not that every possible source of training data was already exhausted.
The capability clause ordinarily means substantive progress had broadly flattened from March 2024 through publication.
The target period runs from the beginning of the named month through the post date.
Substantial gains across several difficult tasks count against a broad capability plateau even if some tasks remain flat. No fixed inference-compute budget is stated.
criteria.support_condition: Credible estimates show an approaching constraint on usable human-produced training text, and comparable evaluations show broadly flattened capability progress from March 2024 through January 29, 2025.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Evidence shows no approaching data constraint, or substantial capability improvements after March 2024. If the two clauses receive different findings, propose mixed and identify which holds.

evidence.explanation: The estimate supports an approaching constraint on usable human-generated public text under continuing scaling trends. It does not show that data was already exhausted, and the discussion identifies other data sources and ways progress could continue.

Using its baseline testing framework, ARC Prize reports public-evaluation scores of 21.2% for o1-preview and 9% for GPT-4o. This is post-March capability progress, although the evaluator also reports substantially greater inference time.

evidence.locator: Evals; supporting comparisons in Appendix A
evidence.explanation: Appendix A reports o1-preview improvements over GPT-4o on mathematics, science and coding, including pass@1 scores of 44.6 versus 9.3 on AIME and 73.3 versus 50.6 on GPQA Diamond. These are developer measurements, but they broaden the evidence beyond a single reasoning benchmark.

METR found limited success on its seven research tasks and no improvement over its best existing model on the autonomy suite. This qualifies the breadth of progress, but METR also warned that its testing could underestimate the models' capabilities.
